> **What this case shows** — older adults sway more: balance declines with age, and fall risk climbs with
> it. This case demonstrates and certifies that across 50 subjects (ages 18–75). Per subject, quiet-standing
> COP path length comes from the **certified** `swayMetrics`; a newly-authored **`correlationTest`** relates
> it to age, reproducing **`scipy.stats.pearsonr`** *and* base R **`cor.test`** **bit-for-bit**. Sway rises
> with age (foam **r = 0.62**, p = 1.5e-6), and the age effect is **stronger on foam** (0.62) than firm
> (0.39) — challenging proprioception unmasks the decline.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — `correlationTest(x, y)` → the correlation coefficient, its p-value and df.
**Way of thinking** — pick the condition that *exposes* the effect. On firm ground healthy adults compensate
and the age signal is muted; on foam, where proprioception is degraded, the age-related decline shows
clearly. The right challenge condition is half the measurement.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioAnalysis::correlationTest()`, `PhysioMoCap::swayMetrics()`.
:::

## Proposition

Across 50 subjects (18–75 y), foam-surface COP path length rises with age (Pearson r = 0.62, p = 1.5e-6,
48 df); the correlation is stronger on foam than firm (0.62 vs 0.39); and `correlationTest` reproduces
`scipy.stats.pearsonr` and base R `cor.test` bit-for-bit.

## Question & goal

**The question is a cohort association and a chained certification: does sway increase with age, is the
effect amplified by a proprioceptive challenge, and does a newly-authored correlation test reproduce the
reference?** The goal is to certify `correlationTest`, reuse the certified `swayMetrics`, and quantify the
age effect.

## Challenge & approach

For each subject we take the age and the eyes-open foam and firm quiet-standing COP path lengths (from
`swayMetrics`, certified against the Prieto reference in the
[sway-posturography-bds](../sway-posturography-bds/index.qmd) case), and correlate age with sway using
`correlationTest`, checking r and p against `scipy.stats.pearsonr` and base R.

```
50 subjects: age, foam sway, firm sway (swayMetrics path length, certified)
  correlationTest(age, foam) → r = 0.62, p = 1.5e-6   vs scipy.stats.pearsonr & base R → |diff| ~1e-16
  correlationTest(age, firm) → r = 0.39   ← weaker: firm ground masks the age decline
```

## Data

**Santos & Duarte (2016) balance dataset (figshare)**: 50 subjects (ages 18–75), one eyes-open foam and one
eyes-open firm quiet-standing trial each (60 s, force-plate COP at 100 Hz). Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: age vs foam-surface COP path length across the 50 subjects, with the regression line — sway climbs with age (r = 0.62, p = 1.5e-6). Right: age vs sway on foam (red) and firm (blue); the foam slope is steeper (r = 0.62 vs 0.39), so a compliant surface amplifies the age-related increase.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* left — the upward trend is the age-related balance decline. Right — both surfaces trend
up with age, but foam rises faster: removing reliable foot-surface cues exposes the deficit older adults
would otherwise compensate for.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| **age vs foam sway** (Pearson r) | **0.62** |
| p-value | 1.5e-6 (−log₁₀ p = 5.8) |
| age vs firm sway (Pearson r) | 0.39 |
| age effect stronger on foam | **yes** |
| vs `scipy.stats.pearsonr` / base R (\|diff\|) | **~1e-16** (bit-for-bit) |

The correlation test equals both references exactly, and the age effect is clear and surface-dependent.
Values trace to [`artifacts/corr_summary.csv`](artifacts/corr_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

`correlationTest` is certified against two references and rests on the already-certified `swayMetrics`.
The transferable takeaway: **postural sway increases with age, and a foam surface — by degrading
proprioception — makes the age-related decline far more visible than firm ground does. This is why
foam-surface posturography is a sensitive probe of the somatosensory contribution to balance, and why
challenge conditions matter for detecting fall risk early.**

## Open questions

- This is a cross-sectional association (not causation) with one trial per subject per surface; a
  longitudinal design would test within-person change, and the BDS's eyes-closed trials, repeats, and full
  metric set would let age be modelled jointly with vision and surface. The foam path length gives the
  clearest single age signal. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Correlation test (Pearson / Spearman) | `correlationTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| Posturography sway metrics | `swayMetrics()` | PhysioMoCap |

**Reading the result.**

- **r and p** — the sign and size of the association plus its significance; report the effect size (r), not
  just the p-value.
- **choose the challenge condition** — an effect muted on firm ground can be clear on foam; the condition
  that exposes the deficit is part of the measurement design.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioAnalysis); library(PhysioMoCap)

sway <- sapply(cop_list, function(cop) swayMetrics(cop, 100)$path_length)  # per subject
correlationTest(age, sway)   # r, p, df -- reproduces scipy.stats.pearsonr and base R cor.test bit-for-bit
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/corr_summary.csv`](artifacts/corr_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py) re-checks the
correlations and p, the bit-exact match against scipy and base R, `df = n − 2`, the positive and
surface-dependent age effect, and the honestly noted scope (new correlation op; inputs from the certified
swayMetrics; cross-sectional association, not causation).
